passages.happening:
The second lot falls to the descendants of Joseph. The writer traces the southern edge of their land. It runs from the Jordan near Jericho, up through the wilderness into the hill country of Bethel, on from Bethel, and down westward past Lower Beth-horon to Gezer, ending at the sea (verses 1-3).

“So Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, received their inheritance” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Joseph was the son of Jacob who was sold into Egypt by his brothers and rose to rule there. On his deathbed Jacob took Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as his own, so that each would count as a tribe. In doing so he set the younger, Ephraim, ahead of the older. This chapter and the next give the two brothers their land, and Ephraim is described first.

The land of Joseph lay in the middle of the country, in the hills north of Judah. It was better watered than Judah's and good for olives and vines.

The border here follows a road the reader has already traveled. The line from the hills down past Beth-horon is the route along which the enemy fled in chapter 10. Places where battles were fought now mark the edges of farms.

Bethel had a long memory attached to it. Jacob slept there as a young man running from home, dreamed of a stairway between earth and heaven, and named the place ‘house of God’. His grandsons' land now reaches to it.

In later centuries Ephraim became the leading tribe of the north. The prophets, Hosea above all, often use its name for the whole northern kingdom.
passages.later:
Jacob's words over the two boys are in Genesis. When Joseph tried to move his father's hand to the older son, Jacob refused: “He too shall become a people, and he too shall be great; nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he” (Genesis 48:19).

The same Jacob had named Bethel: “How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God; this is the gate of heaven!” (Genesis 28:17).
passages.asks: Joseph was sold by his brothers and died in Egypt. Generations later his children received a double share in the heart of the land. Ask what loss in your family's story, or your own, you assume can only ever be a loss. And think about Bethel, where a frightened young man once slept on a stone. Ask what God has built on the places where you were most alone.

passages.t: Ephraim's land, and the Canaanites of Gezer
passages.happening:
The writer gives the borders of Ephraim itself, clan by clan: from Ataroth-addar to Upper Beth-horon, north and east by Michmethath, Taanath-shiloh and Janoah, down to Jericho and the Jordan, and west by the Brook of Kanah to the sea (verses 5-8). Some of Ephraim's towns lay inside the land of Manasseh (verse 9).

The chapter ends as the last one did, with something left undone. “But they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer. So the Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites to this day, but they are forced laborers” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Unlike Judah's chapter, this one has no list of towns. It is short, and its weight falls on the last verse.

The note about towns inside Manasseh shows how the tribes really lived. The lines between them were not walls. Families settled where they could, and a town might belong to one tribe while standing on another's ground.

Gezer was a strong city guarding the road from the coast up into the hills. Its king was among those defeated in chapter 10, but the city itself was not taken. A pharaoh of Egypt lists Gezer among his conquests on a monument from about 1208 BC. The Bible says that Gezer came fully into Israel's hands only in Solomon's time, when a later pharaoh captured it and gave it to his daughter, Solomon's wife.

Forced labor meant work that people were compelled to do for those who ruled them: building, farming, cutting stone. It was common across the ancient world.

Within the book's own terms, what Ephraim did was a failure. Israel had been told to remove the peoples of the land so that their worship would not take root in Israel. Ephraim neither did that nor made an honest peace. It found a third way that paid: let them stay, and make them work. The words ‘to this day’ show that the arrangement lasted.

A reader today will see a second problem, and is right to. Forced labor is itself a wrong. The book reports it and does not praise it. The hard question says more.
passages.later:
The book of Judges repeats the note: “Ephraim also failed to drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer; so the Canaanites continued to dwell among them in Gezer” (Judges 1:29).

Forced labor came back on Israel's own head. King Solomon laid it on his own people, and after his death they said to his son, “Your father put a heavy yoke on us. But now you should lighten the burden of your father’s service and the heavy yoke he put on us, and we will serve you” (1 Kings 12:4). The king refused, and the kingdom split in two.
passages.hard:
Was making the Canaanites of Gezer forced laborers a mercy, a failure or an injustice?

Readers have seen the verse in more than one light.

Within the book, the point is failure. Ephraim had been commanded to drive the Canaanites out and settled for living beside them at a profit. The books that follow show that this kind of arrangement led Israel into the worship of other gods.

From where a modern reader stands, forced labor is troubling in itself, and it is fair to ask how it fits with the law's care for the foreigner and the slave. Some note that the people of Gezer lived, which was more than the ban allowed. Others point out that the Bible remembers Solomon's forced labor as a heavy yoke that helped to break the kingdom.

These notes take the verse as a report of what Ephraim did and not as approval of it. A halfway obedience did not produce a middle path. It produced a second wrong.

Nothing here makes forced labor right. A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ephraim found a way to disobey that also paid. Ask where you have struck a bargain with something God told you to put away, because keeping it is useful. Ask who bears the cost of that bargain. And ask whether there is anyone whose labor you benefit from without ever asking how they are treated.
